en: The Ten Gates of Non-duality from the Profound Record of the Lotus Sutra: Revealing the Subtlety (with Preface).
Composed by the Śramaṇa Shi Chūken of Yongjia.

The teachings of the Sage are sometimes extensive and sometimes concise, as preserved in the various scriptures; yet when one traces the intent behind his transformation of beings, they all ultimately converge upon the Dharma.

The "Flowers" (Huá) refer to the root of the myriad sutras within the Great Canon. Yet, when the Sages appear in the world, they do so fundamentally to guide all sentient beings by means of their own realization.
Because the capacities and dispositions of beings differ, they cannot all be led to the Way at once;

therefore, the Sages employ provisional means (*upāya*) in the beginning and establish the fundamental in the end, causing beings to follow these traces and return to the source. With this sutra, the process is complete. As the text says:
Although various paths were established, their reality is but the Buddha Vehicle; this is specifically intended so that the past may be clearly discerned.

My ancestor personally received this intent and expounded it for ninety days, truly harmonizing with the Sage’s mind. When Jingxi recorded it, he still feared that the text of the Ten Profound Mysteries (*shimiao*) was too voluminous and that the Way of Contemplation was difficult to penetrate.
Thereupon, he extracted the essential principles into the Ten Gates (*shimen*) to indicate the depth of the meaning.

The language is remote and the phrasing, though circuitous, has not been fully detailed in previous commentaries; each adheres to their own views, resulting in a proliferation of divergent arguments that obscure the pure essence.
Not daring to measure my own ignorance against this, I deeply regret [the state of these texts].

Therefore, I have specifically followed the established precedents, setting aside all points of contention to focus exclusively on the essential meaning of the text, providing a new commentary titled *Xianmiao* (Manifesting the Sublime) so as to accord with the intention of the Master of the Record. This is the text.
It is said that from here on, I shall simply set forth the underlying principle so that the purport of this entire scripture may be made as clear as if it were before one's eyes;

for those who take root in this, will they not find it to be so? As for the division of the text, the matching of corresponding passages, and the correction of errors and discrepancies, these existing traditional interpretations need not be discussed further here.

Preface written on the day after the full moon in the eleventh month of winter, in the fourth year of the Xining era of the Great Song dynasty, in the eastern pavilion of the abbot’s quarters at Jingzhu Monastery in Qiantang.
In the *Fahua xuanyi*, the "Ten Non-dual Gates" clarify the wondrous understanding;
however, this Trace Gate discusses its causes and effects as well as self and other.
The profound meaning (*xuanyi*) of these causal and other phenomena is fully detailed therein.
It causes the teachings of a single lifetime to harmonize and enter the subtle.

To directly proclaim this single principle, the intent of the sutra lies herein. Originally, when the Sage bestowed one [teaching] and three [vehicles], the dispositions of sentient beings were roughly distinguished;

yet reaching this point, those dispositions are again subsumed within the subtle principle, so that throughout the entire lifetime of the teaching, the hundred realms are harmonized and all attain Buddhahood through world-transcending liberation.
The general meaning is exhaustively expressed herein.
Therefore, all explanations of the various doctrines are based upon the Four Teachings and the Five Flavors.

By contrasting the provisional teachings and flavors within this single lifetime, the Buddha employs skillful means to guide and lead sentient beings, enabling their faculties to realize the Subtle. If one can truly understand this...
The "wondrous" (*miao*) is precisely the realization that this is opening; how could one allow for seeking it elsewhere?
The intent lies in opening the teachings so that all may enter the *amṛta* (the supreme essence).

Realizing the wondrous and opening the coarse involves a relative distinction of teaching-flavors, yet all become transcendent. Even transcendence is beyond description; how much less could one remain stuck in it?
A rough judgment might conclude that there is no fault greater than this; yet for over forty years, its true purport has not been fully elucidated.
Now that this sutra has been revealed, the Sage’s intention is uniquely manifest: the wondrous teaching is the cream of the cream, and mind, Buddha, and sentient beings are one.
Contemplating the mind (*citta-vipaśyanā*) is the pivotal mechanism of both teaching and practice; for now, it shall be briefly indicated by way of various expositions.

Having already opened up the wondrous understanding above, which integrates the entire lifetime of the Buddha’s teachings, we now demonstrate the application of that understanding through contemplating the mind. When the whole mind is contemplation, this is precisely what is called "wondrous contemplation.
If it were not for this contemplation of the mind, how could the teaching be established? Upon what could practice depend? Therefore, it is said that contemplating the mind is [the core].
The teaching and practice are the pivot and mechanism. Since the teaching is already pure, perfect, and subtle, practice must necessarily eliminate all delusions and afflictions;

this is what is meant by "establishing practice based upon the teaching. Thus, the Master of the Commentary (Zhiyi) said: "The ten realms, such as the realm of the five aggregates, exist only within the three teachings.

Formerly it was said that in contrast to the partial [teachings], the Perfect and Constant Teaching lacks them; however, even in the case of the relative, the subtle teaching has its coarse summit in the past.
How could it be that the absolute, perfect fusion is instead found within the deluded mind? To give a name to this while the name itself is incorrect—where can one’s practice be entrusted?
Whether [the teaching] is preserved or lost is not the primary intent of this school.

Although the practice gates (xingmen) are essential, they are not the primary subject of discussion here; thus, their presence or absence varies. Only when one focuses specifically on the treatises of calming and contemplation (zhiguan) are the characteristics of the practices fully prepared.
Therefore, even if there are arrangements that rely on phenomena or attach to dharmas, or that analyze the ten contemplations, these merely list the names.

Contemplation (*vipaśyanā*) is precisely the mind; subject and object are non-dual, and the principle transcends contemplation, for its meaning is perfected. Furthermore, what are the aggregates (*skandha*)? Now, regarding the great meaning of contemplation, there are only these three types:
either "entrusting to phenomena" (*vastu-pratītya*), which relies on contemplation to perceive principle; or "attaching to practice," which follows the dharma—the other two types are likewise so.

Although the meaning is thus divided into three types of contemplation, the fundamental text speaks of only one: contemplating the mind (*citta-vipaśyanā*). While this is not the primary [method], it is the root.

Since these three characteristics are fully present, they are set forth here; moreover, because the Fifth Patriarch personally received the transmission, he was able to comprehend the intent of the teachings of an entire era.
Taking the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* as his fundamental principle, he described the essentials of the text solely through teaching (*śāsana*) and contemplation (*vipaśyanā*).

The Master of Records attained the profound meaning and deeply accorded with the patriarchal transmission; the establishment of this teaching and contemplation is exhausted in these few phrases, which cut to the very root of the source of transformation.
Regarding the essential intent of this commentary, there may be instances where the teaching and contemplation are not properly aligned in their application.

What is clarified here concerns the principles, objects, wisdom, practices, stages, and dharmas—both the means of transformation and those transformed. The underlying purpose lies in the capacity for expression; within that expression, all things are wondrous.
To distinguish these, I shall elucidate the beginning and end of the process of self-transformation within the realm of expression.

Having provided this general summary above, what follows below presents the specific details; as the general and the specific mutually illuminate one another, the Sage’s intent becomes even more manifest.

Although the main text discusses extensively the objects of cognition (*ālambana*), wisdom (*jñāna*), and self-manifestation (*svapariṇāma*), it first reveals the teaching that serves as the means of expression (*vyañjana*).

Since the wondrous skillful means of this teaching of expression constitutes the general principle for the entire work, what dharma is considered "wondrous"? It is precisely the objects of cognition and wisdom, from beginning to end.
He manifested his wondrous marks to himself and others;
therefore, he fully expounded the ten wonders, encompassing the great purport of the world-transcending transformation without exception.

Since the great purport of the world-transcending [teaching] arose as the "wonderful," and now that the wonderful has been discussed exhaustively, it is the intent of the Buddha. As for this "intent of the Buddha":

Regarding the nature of sentient beings, since the teaching is expounded based on their fundamental nature, how could there be any further separate teaching? Contemplation and the teaching are of one accord;

the true reality (*dharmatā*) of all phenomena is the omnipresent body of Vairocana. Such is the meaning of the scriptural text. When cause and effect are both wondrous, the beginning and the end are severed, the coarse is transcended, the work of transformation is complete, and the intent is exhausted therein.
Therefore, one must not fail to comprehend the general outline of the ten wonders.

As for this general outline of the ten wonders, only a Buddha has fully realized it; yet if a beginner attains it, how would they differ from a Buddha? That sentient beings open the Buddha’s knowledge and vision depends on this.
Those who receive this teaching must certainly be thus, even if they possess only the physical eye; they are then said to be [possessing the Dharma-eye].
The Buddha-eye is its verification.
Therefore, I have extracted the Ten Profundities as the general framework for the method of contemplation.

If one thoroughly understands these ten profundities, this very understanding of the mind constitutes the essence of the great function of contemplation; by employing this to engage with objects, there will be nothing that is not true.
In truth, the constant contemplation of the characteristics of the world accords with the scriptures; the words and meanings correspond.
If one understands that both the trace and the source are wondrous, one should know that they are not distant from one another, differing only in their being separated or joined.
Since the meaning of cause and effect is one, how can self and other be different? Therefore, the text below states: "Though the source and the trace differ, they are inconceivably one."

Since the manifested traces have already reached the level of the subtle, how could they differ from the fundamental? Although their separation and union differ, the subtle principle is fundamentally the same;
the evidence cited is clear and should be recognized with faith.
Furthermore, essence, doctrine, and function are merely the phenomena of self and other, cause and effect; moreover, the characteristics of the teachings are merely conceptual distinctions.
The preceding four chapters render these four distinct from all other texts forever.

Having already explained that the names and the fundamental and manifested traces (*honji-suijaku*) are entirely equal, and that the four chapters are no different from the names—taking these three together as the essence of the name and so forth—how could they differ?
To cite one example shall suffice for all; there is no need to exhaustively list them all.
If one understands this principle, then the teachings will have their ultimate destination.
Although the sutras establish various paths, they are in fact for the sake of the Buddha-vehicle (Buddhayāna). What is this Buddha-vehicle? It is nothing other than the wondrous.
"Periods (ki) are both vertical and horizontal.
"Period" (ki) is synonymous with "generation" (tei); one generation constitutes both the vertical and the horizontal. "Vertical" refers to time, while "horizontal" refers to the teachings.

Regarding the manifest discourse prior to the *Lotus Sūtra*, the vertical and horizontal were already established, yet beings remained unaware of where they were headed. Now that this sūtra has appeared to manifest the discourse on returning to the source, the multitude [have found their destination].
The heart is struck with awe as the wondrous teaching arises and the Great Matter is revealed; this shall be seen in the subsequent text.
Not departing from a single thought-moment, the three thousand worlds are themselves emptiness, the provisional, and the middle.

This directly proclaims the sublime purport and manifests the Buddha-vehicle: that the three thousand worlds within a single thought-moment are themselves emptiness, the provisional, and the middle. It is found right here.

Now, whenever a single thought arises, it must necessarily confront a single object; the mind does not contemplate multiple objects simultaneously, but arises in pursuit of them, with arising and ceasing shifting and succeeding one another without ever being abandoned for even a moment.
Although the various teachings of the provisional vehicles may sever [delusion], they cannot eliminate its root;

thus, the objective realm and the subjective mind still coexist with those teachings. Since these remain interwoven both vertically and horizontally, the wondrous nature remains unmanifest. Now, I shall point to this one...

Contemplating how the three thousand realms share the same identity as this single thought-moment—this single thought is the principle, and the three thousand worlds are themselves emptiness, provisionality, and the Middle Way.
This perfectly accords with the nature of thought; when the root of thought is eliminated, even true reality is eternally severed, so how could delusion remain?
When both truth and delusion have subsided, the gate of non-duality opens, and one enters the Buddha-realm where all phenomena in their true aspect are without the distinction of the three truths.
The single nature is entirely identical; it is inherently possessed by all living beings and is not something produced through effort. This is the profound inner sanctum of the wondrous Dharma.

Those of superior faculties enter directly and immediately ascend to the first stage (*prathamabhūmi*). Whether horizontal or vertical, all phenomena return to the source. When one door returns to its origin, all doors do likewise. This is solely a matter of grasping the essential meaning;
one must guard against clinging to emotional attachments or becoming bound by literal words while claiming to have attained full realization.
It is like seeking fish by climbing a tree; there is no principle by which one could obtain them.
This applies equally to principles, objects, and even benefits.

Since this is the case regarding both objects and principles, the nine subsequent sections [of this treatise] rely upon these ten dharmas—all of which are sublime and constitute the Buddha Vehicle. Thus is the title of the present sutra.
By establishing these sublime names,

the ten vehicles of calming and contemplation (*śamatha-vipaśyanā*) constitute the cause and effect of one's own practice (*sva-caryā*), while the chapter on "arousing the teaching" constitutes the agent and object of transforming others (*parārtha*).
The word "then" (*ze*) connects to the preceding phrase; thus, one understands that the ten vehicles of *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā* constitute the cause and fruit of one's own practice.

When this chapter on the arousal of the teaching is employed to transform others, the relationship between the agent and the object of transformation is such that the names and meanings of the two sections are seen to be consistent.

Thus, both [the teaching and the practice] become clearly manifest; the practice of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* is perfected, ensuring that one's efforts are not in vain and that what is expounded can be understood.

By illuminating and making things manifest, one perfects the practice through the teaching and supports the practice with the teaching, so that effort is not in vain—this is because the teaching and practice are present herein.
Since this is what is expounded, it is said that "it can be understood."
Therefore, the ten wonders are further subsumed within ten gates.

If one wishes to instruct others to accomplish practice, there is no gate through which they will not enter; since the teaching is already wondrous, how could the practice based upon that teaching follow a different path?
Thus, the subsequent text states: "The ten gates are restated so that contemplative practice may be recognized."
What is meant by "expediently applying the Real, the non-dual becomes dual," and "opening the expedient to reveal the Real, the dual becomes non-dual"?

Speaking of the intent behind establishing the transformation according to this present sutra: when the Real is applied as the expedient, the entirety of the Real becomes the expedient; when the expedient is opened to reveal the Real, the entirety of the expedient is the Real.
The wondrous non-duality of the expedient and the Real lies at the source of transformation. Taking this as the gateway, one enters the Buddha-vehicle, just as one uses a finger to point at the moon.
All the palm-prints.
Since the teachings and divisions of the Dharma have all been opened and perfected into the wondrous, these ten gates are titled "Non-duality.
If one does not find the gate to the palace, one will not see the beauty of the ancestral temple; likewise, if one does not find the gate to the Ultimate Way, [one will not perceive its splendor].

Beholding the profound depths of the wondrous Dharma Hall, where non-duality serves as the gate, how could emotional views be tolerated? If the gate is established yet one does not see [the truth], whose fault is it?
At each and every gate, one should examine this by means of the six stages of realization.

Since the gates have already been established as the wondrous entry for those who attain Buddhahood, each gate is examined through the six stages of realization (*liu ji*) to reveal the relative heights of the Buddhas, thereby preventing the conflation of the merit of one gate with that of another.

The preceding text has already extensively cited authentic proofs; hereafter, I shall simply set forth the underlying principle directly, so that the purport of this entire scripture may become clear.

In the present moment, this single principle is direct and straightforward, not difficult to realize; that the essential aim does not lie in other paths is evident before one’s eyes—how could it be empty talk?
First is the gate of the non-duality of form and mind; second is the gate of the non-duality of the internal and external; third is the gate of the non-duality of cultivation and nature.
The four gates are: first, the gate of the non-duality of cause and effect; second, the gate of the non-duality of defilement and purity;
third, the gate of the non-duality of the environment and its inhabitants; fourth, the gate of the non-duality of self and others; fifth, the gate of the non-duality of the three karmas;

sixth, the gate of the non-duality of provisional and ultimate truth; seventh, the gate of the non-duality of receiving and moistening. Among these, the first derives its name from the excellence of the objective realm.
The second and third are named after their wisdom and conduct; the fourth is named after its stage and dharma;
the fifth, sixth, and seventh are named after their responsive transformations and supernormal powers; the eighth and ninth are named after their preaching of the Dharma;
and the tenth is named after its retinue and benefits.
The ten "Marvelous Gates" differ in their number according to the convenience of their respective meanings;
yet, while each follows its own meaning, they do not forget the fundamental number and all establish ten.
First, regarding the Gate of the Non-duality of Matter and Mind: for each of the ten such as the "Ten Suchnesses of Objects" up to the "Ultimate Truth," there is a general [summary].
The two distinct meanings are unified within a single thought-moment (*ekacitta*). Form and mind (*rūpa-citta*) are distinguished separately;

yet, within the single gateway of form and mind, they are established as "sublime" (*miao*) according to their objects. These objects comprise seven categories of dharmic characteristics (*dharmalakṣaṇa*), which are extremely extensive;

now, however, they are subsumed under the categories of form and mind. The manner of this subsumption will be evident from the text below. As for the distinction between form and mind, they are non-dual (*advaya*).
The formation of the two delusive objects is such that their essence is one; this "two" is precisely the wondrous gate of "non-two.

Therefore, by means of the ten gates—both general and specific, and through the severance of all extremes—the characteristics of duality and non-duality are made clearly manifest, so that the essential purport of the gates is not obstructed.
Thus we know that the wondrous gate of the non-duality of objects resides in the single thought-moment; when the essence of form and mind is realized as one, this is attained.
The gate of the Jewel Vehicle is itself the site of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*); once this first [gate] is thus understood, the remaining nine gates follow by extension through analogy.
This penetration requires no further reflection. Why?

Because within the initial ten [aspects], characteristics reside solely in form (*rūpa*), while nature resides solely in the essence of mind; the functions and powers encompass the meaning of serving as conditions.
The causes and effects of form and mind, as well as the retribution of the mind-only, pertain exclusively to form.

These ten "suchnesses" (tathatā) distinguish between form and mind; the six objects discussed below are likewise distinguished and contrasted with respect to form and mind, each according to its specific meaning, as detailed in the text.

In the twelve links of dependent origination, suffering and karma both encompass both afflictions and the mind, while delusion resides solely in the mind. Regarding the four truths, three encompass both form and mind, while cessation resides solely in the mind.
Of the two truths, three truths are conventional and comprise both form and mind; the true and the middle truths are mental-only.
This can be understood by analogy with the one reality and the absence of truth.

Thus, having established the correspondence between these two through the seven categories of dharmic characteristics, both are now seen as the objective realm (viṣaya) and the subjective mind (citta).

True Suchness (tathatā), by following conditions, manifests as the nine realms, whereby Buddha-nature becomes obscured and the gate of non-duality is closed. Now, this objective realm is revealed so that one may understand the characteristics of the deluded mind;

this serves as the fundamental basis for entering the gate of non-duality below. Furthermore, the "True" and the "Middle" are both the single reality, which is the realm of principle (li). Why is this?

Although the existence of method within emotion belongs to the realm of principle, it is present in relation to emotion; however, by destroying that emotion, one returns to nature at once, as can be seen in the subsequent text.
Once the distinctions are known, the distinct is subsumed into the general.
Having already known the distinctions, one binds them to the supreme; this subsumes the particulars into the universal, giving rise to the subsequent [realization]:
all phenomena are none other than the nature of mind; in this single nature that is without inherent nature, the three thousand worlds are perfectly manifest.

This is the explanation of the general characteristic (*sāmānya-lakṣaṇa*). Having already demonstrated the specific characteristics (*viśeṣa-lakṣaṇa*) above, "discernment" (*vijñapti*) is now presented as the general characteristic;
thus, it is directly shown that all phenomena are none other than the nature of mind. This is precisely the inclusion of the specific within the general, for the general is itself the nature.
Consequently, the seven categories [of dharmas] all become non-dual. This very point is the gateway through which one reaches the Buddha-vehicle; the Buddha is necessarily threefold.

The body points to the three marks (trilakṣaṇa) to manifest the one wondrous essence within the mind-nature: the middle is the emptiness of nature, and the three thousand [realms] are the provisional.

Therefore it is said: "As for the three truths, they are the innate, inherent virtue. Now, taking this as the gateway, those of superior faculties enter directly into the first stage (prathamābhūmi) through a single contemplation;
or else, through the inner and outer stages of the ordinary person (pṛthagjana). The wondrous principle of the three truths remains thus from beginning to end.
The essential purport of the various sections of the sutras is consistent from beginning to end; if one understands this gate, it will not be difficult when reaching the subsequent sections.

One should know that the "matter of mind" (citta-rūpa) is simply the mind itself, which is termed "transformation" (*pariṇāma*); "transformation" is termed "conditioning" (*nirmāṇa*), and "conditioning" refers to essence and function.

This extensive commentary explains the two aforementioned alternative names. That which is above, the "upper part," consists of form and mind; this is simply one transformation of the nature of mind into the duality of form and mind.
These two delusions are not distinct; the entirety of delusion is the realization of the True. This is also termed "phenomenal creation" (*shizao*) and "deluded function.
It is always the case that the entire water becomes waves; this is shown here as an analogy. Thus it is demonstrated.
This means that while it is neither matter nor mind, yet it is both matter and mind; that it is exclusively matter and exclusively mind is precisely due to this.

This is a further explanation of how the deluded is realized as the true. Since the truly real has already fully manifested as the deluded, by fully realizing the deluded, one fully realizes the true.
Thus, the three obstructions are themselves the three virtues (*triguṇa*); water is the element of moisture, and all things are thereby perfected. Therefore, it is neither matter nor [mind].
When the mind descends to seal the three truths, they become manifest; that they are perfectly interwoven and mutually constitutive is precisely due to this.
Thus one should know that by simply recognizing a single thought-moment, one sees universally both oneself and others, as well as the Buddhas and sentient beings of all lifetimes.

Since even the Buddhas and sentient beings of other lifetimes are identical with the mind, how much more so the Buddhas and sentient beings of one’s own life who could possibly deviate from this single thought-moment?
If, as this consciousness shows, a single thought-moment is entirely the nature of the three virtues, and self and others, birth and buddhahood, are precisely this very thought-moment,
then for the practitioner— if this is so— from whom would a Buddha arise?
Therefore, regarding those various objects and phenomena, they are both differentiated and non-differentiated.

Since the three dharmas have not yet reached the present state, their differentiation is established; yet this very differentiation is non-differentiation, whereby the sublime name becomes even more manifest.
Second, as for the Gate of the Non-duality of Internal and External: whatever object one contemplates does not transcend the internal or the external.
The division of internal and external realms is established solely in relation to the delusory objects of observation; it does not mean that non-duality itself is divided into internal and external.
As the text says: "Delusion is called internal and external, while awakening is but the one mind.

Nevertheless, regarding the characteristics of these three dharmas, whenever internal and external are established according to the specific features of various phenomena in all preceding scriptures, they have all been rendered untenable by the present sutra.
Both of these can enter into principle, and thus principle is called the "gate.

"External" refers to relying upon the phenomenal forms and mind of the dependent and the supporting; because these are wondrously empty, provisional, and middle, the substance of form and mind is transcendent, being solely the single true nature, wherein there is no emptiness, provisionality, or middle.

Relying upon those [phenomena] of the environment and its inhabitants, one establishes external form and mind; now, realizing that these objects are the wondrous mystery of emptiness, provisionality, and the Middle, these very objects are transcended as being of a single nature.

Since even the characteristics of emptiness, provisionality, and the Middle must be without form, how could this wondrous nature—which stands forth in its own right—be established in opposition to anything as "external" environment or inhabitants?
Form and mind are vividly present, suddenly opening up to be identical with true purity; there are no longer any sentient beings, nor any distinctions among the seven stages of expedient means.
One does not perceive the differences between pure and impure lands.

Form and mind are vividly present, identical with true clarity and purity; they accord with the wondrous aggregate of emptiness, such that there are no longer any sentient beings or distinctions between pure and impure lands.
The environment and its inhabitants, as well as the physical and mental aspects, are all simultaneously extinguished, such that all external appearances are empty and pure;
yet the sovereign thread of reality, both in its environment and inhabitants, remains eternally radiant.

By gathering these [appearances] together, they are immediately established, and this wondrous provisional nature is thus perfected. Although the explanations may appear sequential, they are perfectly integrated, being directly revealed as a single simultaneous whole.
The gate of principle is thus.

As for what is called "internal," one first realizes that external forms are, in a single thought-moment, non-thought; that the internal essence alone is the three thousand [realms], which are themselves empty, provisional, and middle.

If even a single thought-moment exists, internal and external become separated; yet when not lost for even a kṣaṇa, matter and mind are of one essence, and the perfect nature is fully present as the three thousand realms—emptiness, the provisional, and the middle.
This means that external phenomena are entirely the nature of the mind; since the nature of the mind has no exterior, its encompassing is all-pervading, reaching the Buddhas of the ten directions.
The nature and substance of sentient beings within the dharma-realm are without distinction and all-pervasive.
Once deluded thoughts are eliminated, the external is identical to the internal; since even the oneness of the Buddhas with this nature cannot be established, how could a duality be posited?
Since all things are entirely pervasive, how could they be produced through intentional effort?

Who would say that there are distinctions between internal and external, matter and mind, or self and other? This is precisely accomplished by means of the "Gate of the Non-duality of Matter and Mind.
Since this wondrous principle is a single, unified whole, what could possibly be amiss in using that to establish this?

Third, regarding the Gate of the Non-duality of Practice and Nature: The nature-virtue (*prakṛti-guṇa*) is precisely the *dharmadhātu* within a single thought-moment; herein, the *dharmadhātu* is fully endowed with the three dharmas.
This is what is called the "perfectly interfused Three Truths" as nature, and the "eternal bliss" of each [truth] as virtue. The ultimate principle of this nature-virtue is precisely...
The realms are like moments of thought, their traces severed in every instant; taking this as the gateway, cultivation and nature are non-dual from beginning to end.
Although nature is thus by its very essence, it relies upon wisdom to give rise to cultivation.

The preceding has clarified nature; this treatise now addresses cultivation. There is no cultivation separate from the understanding of nature: the mind that understands nature is itself called cultivation.

Observing the lower [stages] where cultivation reaches its consummation, the term "cultivation" (*bhāvanā*) is established; though the names are the same, their meanings differ. They accord with goodness and lead to clear penetration, and thus must not be treated as identical.
Through cultivation, one illuminates the nature; through the nature, cultivation is brought forth.
The same substance illuminates and gives rise [to phenomena], mutually supporting one another; this does not harm the nature of cultivation, for it is the natural, wondrous principle.

When abiding in the nature, the entirety of cultivation is perfected within the nature; when cultivation arises from the nature, the entirety of the nature is perfected through cultivation. The nature undergoes no shift, yet cultivation remains ever-vivid.
When the entirety of nature is perfected through cultivation, nature undergoes no displacement; when the entirety of cultivation is perfected as nature, cultivation remains ever manifest.
Although the names "cultivation" and "nature" distinguish their aspects, their substance is eternally non-dual.
There are two kinds of cultivation: cultivation in accordance with the natural order and cultivation in reverse order.
There are two kinds of cultivation that must be distinguished as either "conformable" or "contrary" to avoid confusion.
"Conformable" refers to taking the realization of one's nature as practice; "contrary" refers to turning one's back on one's nature to create delusion.
If one takes realization as practice, how could practice differ from nature? To treat cultivation as being separated from nature by heaven is a grave error.
In delusion and awakening, although the two minds are non-dual, the natures of the two—contrary and compliant—are eternally distinct in their phenomenal reality.
While the nature remains the same in both delusion and awakening, the phenomena of the contrary and compliant differ.
Because the phenomenon does not shift the mind, one must cause the practice of delusion to become perfected through realization.
How could one possibly mistake "delusion" and "awakening" for being the same, such that one claims the deluded mind itself is awakening? This would be a great error;
therefore, this is specifically pointed out. Thus, throughout a single period, one must take delusion and awakening as the illumination of the nature to constitute cultivation.
One must distinguish the mind that illuminates its own nature and demonstrate it as clarity.

When both the cultivation of seeing one's nature and the cultivation of the mind are extinguished, since seeing one's nature is itself without nature, how could cultivation be established again? If one does not understand nature, by what means could cultivation be extinguished?
Furthermore, one understands that the cultivation of the nature of accordance (shun-xiu) involves both separation and union.
Setting aside the contrary, when one accords with principle, the characteristics of separation and union are necessarily wondrously integrated and accomplished through accordance with principle.
"Separation" refers to the three aspects each of cultivation and nature; "union" refers to two aspects of cultivation and one aspect of nature.
That cultivation and nature are each complete in three aspects is the state of their separation; that cultivation and nature are paired together as three is the aspect of their union.
Separation and union occur simultaneously without the slightest interval; nature and cultivation are one in essence, never for a moment distinct.
This text on the wondrous nature and its inconceivable purport is spontaneous and natural—how could it be grasped through emotional views?
Because of this differentiation, it is ultimately said that they are of one characteristic of union; the analogy of waves and water is fully explained in the subsequent text.
Regarding the cultivation of the two [aspects], each has three, which together give rise to the three natures; thus, although the cultivation comprises nine times nine, it is in fact only three.

Although the "capable of producing" and the "produced" each have three aspects, there are nine in total; these nine are merely three [pairs], and their separation is itself the manifestation of their non-dual union.
To clarify the cultivation (bhāvanā) in contrast to the intrinsic nature (prakṛti), cultivation is combined into two.
Although they are distinguished as separate when analyzed according to their meanings, this analytical distinction does not contradict their wondrous principle of nature.

Although the nature [of the mind] is paired with the conditions of the object and the faculty, there is no effort in cultivation; thus, they are spoken of as one through their union. Although cultivation involves both desire and capacity, because it manifests their functional ability, only two are discussed.
Yet, although these are analytically distinguished, their essence is eternally one.
The two and the one are of the same nature, like water being waves; the two are also non-dual, just as waves are water.
The analogy of waves and water is intimate and easily discernible; since the nature and the One Vehicle are like waves and water, the phenomena and principle of the dual cultivation are likewise so.
May you understand through this analogy and examine this meaning in detail.
One should know that "nature" (prakṛti) refers to the three obstructions; therefore, by possessing the three cultivations, one accomplishes the three dharmas from nature as their natural result.
If cultivation lacked nature, it would be like a tree without roots. If the Buddha lacked this foundation, how could he have been accomplished?
Since the original source is wondrous and beyond illness, one need not seek it; yet when sought, it is immediately attained—how could anything surpass this?
Realizing that the nature of non-cultivation is the single, wondrous vehicle, one is free from all discrimination; the Dharma-realm is thus transparently luminous.

That "realizing the nature of non-cultivation" leads to "transparent luminosity" means that although the phrasing occurs here, the meaning actually extends back to the preceding discussion on cultivation and nature.

How could it be that one has not yet realized [this truth] and is still making distinctions? Thus, we know that when speaking truly of nature and cultivation, there is in fact nothing to be grasped or rejected.
When all conceptual discriminations have vanished, the Dharma-realm is eternally luminous; its wondrous non-dual aspect is one reality from beginning to end.
Though words may appear to come before or after, if one remains thus deluded by the emotions, one cannot discuss the Way. Only when one understands this clearly can the Way be discussed.
This is established through the gate of the non-duality of the internal and external; as for the gate of the non-duality of the four causes and effects:
since the mind of sentient beings—the cause—already possesses the three tracks, this cause, when perfected as a fruit, is called the three nirvāṇas.
The non-duality of cause and effect likewise points entirely to the wondrous principle that a single thought-moment is fully endowed with the three tracks (*tri-vidhi*).
Thus we know that if one does not point to the three tracks, there is no way to shatter the thought-moment; since the thought-moment is not shattered, cause and effect remain eternally distinct.

When one realizes that the thought-moment is itself the principle, cause and effect are both equalized. If one attains this realization, all ten gates are established; therefore, the Gate of Matter and Mind states: "All are contained therein."

If one distinguishes matter and mind within a single thought-moment, this may likewise be illustrated by saying that while they are collectively contained within a single thought-moment, they are individually distinguished as cause and effect.
One must not allow the mind to stagnate in these various gates of cause and effect, which are both identical and distinct.

Since there is no difference between cause and effect and the principle of beginning and end is one, if the qualities of the fruit are already complete within the cause, why does it not abide in the state of the cause?
This arises from the single principle [of dependent origination] up to this doubt: if the cause is already fully present and the causal condition is sufficient, why establish a separate effect?
Why would the cause be altered upon receiving the effect? Wherein lies the excellence of the causal condition?
It is merely due to delusion regarding the cause that each person claims it to be real; if one understands the nature of delusion, reality is simply the abiding of the cause.
Deluded attachment consists in regarding cause and effect as truly distinct natures. One might ask: "If they abide [as one], what difference is there between cause and effect?
Therefore, when one investigates this cause for a long time, the cause manifests and is called 'effect.
Since it abides as the cause, why does a perfected person further establish the designation 'effect'? To this, the explanation is: "It is simply through long-term investigation..."
This cause is designated as "fruit" because it manifests [the fruit]; there is no separate fruit apart from it.
Since the principle of cause and fruit is one, this single principle serves as the causal principle; once the causal principle is manifested, the name "fruit" no longer exists.
How could the designation of "cause" still be maintained?
If one discerns it, there is not even the slightest discrepancy; if one loses it, from beginning to end and from root to branch, it is all one.
Only when this is realized can the six sense bases all be called the Buddha.

Since cause and effect have dissolved, the rational nature naturally vanishes; it is solely due to the loss of wisdom and the resulting distinctions between the near and the distant that delusion becomes thick or thin.

Thus, delusion becomes wisdom; the depth or shallowness of this wisdom depends on the thickness or thinness of delusion. This thickness or thinness is measured by the degree of delusion, while wisdom is always perfect and complete.
Because delusion is thick or thin, it is forcefully divided into three grades of affliction (*kleśa*), which open into six stages; these are precisely what are called the varying depths of wisdom.

Is it not the case that delusion is fundamentally one, yet divided into three according to its thickness? Is it not the principle that while the function remains the same, the substance differs—namely, the meaning of thickness versus thinness and depth versus shallowness?
Therefore, as in a dream, if one exerts diligent effort, the empty name of "delusion" will cease.
Although practice is like a dream and cannot be abandoned for even a moment, and although delusion is a mere empty name, it does not cease without practice;
through diligent cultivation, the characteristics of depth and shallowness are perfected. This is because, in accord with reality, all things are like illusions.

The cause of illusion being fulfilled, the fruit of the mirror-image is complete; though the empty image and the [illusory] image share the same meaning, the former is empty while the latter is substantial.

Although the names "empty" and "mirror-image" are identical in their referent, the states of delusion and awakening, as well as the substantial and the insubstantial, are separated by their respective natures.
Because the image is real, it is called the principle; because the void is fundamentally empty, delusion revolves to form its nature.
When the image manifests, it is called the principle; the entire nature is fully present. Since the infinite void is fundamentally non-existent, it revolves according to the light of wisdom.
This is the case where non-duality appears as duality, establishing cause and effect as distinct; yet though dual, they are non-dual, for their essence is one from beginning to end.

If one were to claim that the cause differs from the effect, then the cause would not truly be a cause; it is only by understanding that the effect proceeds from the cause that the cause can then produce the effect.
Without the cause of the true reality, there can be no attainment of the fruit of perfect consummation; as the form is upright, the shadow is straight, so it is with the mind at its inception.
Thus, when the three thousand realms abide in principle, they are collectively termed ignorance; when the three thousand realms are realized as the fruit, they are all called eternal bliss.

In a single moment of thought, the hundred realms arise together as ignorance; in a single instant of attachment to the faculties, the three thousand worlds are all called "eternal, blissful, self, and pure.
The Sutra says: "Ordinary beings and sages are equal, with no high or low; it depends only on whether the mind is defiled or pure.
To realize the truth is like turning over the palm of one's hand; if the thought [of delusion] persists, it is like not turning the palm over."
The three thousand [realms] undergo no alteration; ignorance is itself enlightenment. The three thousand are simultaneously eternal, both in essence and in function.
The *Jinbei* states: "These three thousand natures are the Middle Way; they should not be regarded as existent or non-existent, for existence and non-existence are naturally so.
If one can perceive them in their entirety, the thoughts that constitute ignorance above are all the essence and function of ultimate enlightenment—an indivisible unity.
The principle is likewise derived from this: the preceding four sections all state that only through the three thousand [realms] does one perceive the One, and not two.
This is established by the "Gate of the Non-duality of Cultivation and Nature.
These four gates above encompass the causes and fruits of one's own practice within a single moment of mind; this perfect contemplation can be understood as follows.
The manner in which the six gates encompass the characteristics of transforming others may be understood by analogy with the preceding intent.
Regarding the fifth gate, the Non-duality of Defilement and Purity:

how could the characteristics of defilement and purity be otherwise than they are? It is merely due to the delusion or awakening of sentient beings' faculties; therefore, the following passage states:

Is this not what is meant by saying that although the three thousand realms have not yet been manifested and verified, one remains deluded regarding their essence? If delusive sentiments are removed, the pure aspect will naturally manifest.
If one realizes that from the beginningless past the dharma-nature has been ignorance, then one can understand that now ignorance is itself the dharma-nature.
If one knows that beginningless ignorance is entirely the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*), how could it not be so for present ignorance?

Present ignorance resides within the nature of phenomena; because one fails to know this, ignorance finds its opportunity. It may even lead one to realize that the entire dharma-realm is delusively taken as the self and the essence of wisdom.
Thus, regarding the correspondence between defilement and purity according to the capacity of beings, one need not feel shame over even a hair’s breadth of error, for it is naturally so.
Thus it is accomplished.
When the nature of phenomena (dharmatā) and ignorance (avidyā) universally create all dharmas, this is termed "defilement";
when ignorance and the nature of phenomena universally respond to various conditions, this is termed "purity."

Because defilement and purity share the same substance and respond according to conditions, the various Buddhas within the minds of sentient beings are moved by them, and the Buddhas respond to the capacities of sentient beings within their own minds;
thus, the interaction between the response and the stimulus is like a voice answering an echo.
Turbid water and clear water are no different in their moisture and wetness;

although clarity and turbidity arise from conditions, when used as a metaphor for transformation, if one realizes that the nature of moisture is pure, how could the turbid be any different from the clear?
Thus, the principle of the mutual interaction of the Way and its response can be understood through this analogy.
Yet turbidity is inherently present from the beginning;
the capacities of sentient beings have never been separated from or united with it since time immemorial.
Although turbidity is inherently present, its entire substance is pure, for according to the principle of the two waves, the whole essence is universally functioning.
Since the principle of *paratantra* (dependent origination) pervades both essence and function such that they are entirely one, how could it be otherwise?

Therefore, the three thousand [realms] are all termed dependent origination in terms of cause and effect; the dependent origination of delusion and enlightenment is not separate from a single moment (*kṣaṇa*).

This illustrates that the essence of the dharmas, when combined with the two preceding waters, reveals that their nature is no different; the nature seen in each moment and the principle of dependent origination are entirely identical.
The nature of each moment is eternal, and the principle of dependent origination is one.
Seeing that the substance of nature is one is like waves whose principle is pervasive, uniting the beginning, the end, and the middle; this can be understood by analogy.
Within the single principle, one distinguishes between the pure and the defiled.

In a single kṣaṇa, as soon as one realizes that the nature itself is divided into the pure and the defiled, one perceives that the hundred realms are contained within the mind and the three thousandfold world is one's own self.
Specifically, there are six defilements and four purities; generally, there are ten that encompass both purity and defilement.

While the six defilements and four purities are distinguished directly according to the ten realms, the ten that encompass both purity and defilement are established by mutually relating them across the hundred realms.

Although these specific and general categories are no different from the equality of the nature of a single kṣaṇa, their ultimate aim points toward the wondrous realm as it emerges from the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra*.
These words clarify this point.

Therefore, one should know that although the essence of the defiled state in each *kṣaṇa* is entirely pure, because the three thousand worlds have not yet been manifested and verified, one remains deluded;
thus, in the stage of "semblance," the six sense organs achieve universal illumination, and the ten realms within each organ are clearly and distinctly manifest.
Awakening reveals delusion; if delusion has not yet been resolved, it persists from moment to moment. By perceiving the nature (dharmatā) in each moment, the defiled substance is purified.

How is this nature purified? When the three thousand natures are understood according to this principle, one then accords with the original sūtra’s teaching that all phenomena are eternally without self-nature.

How could those with the six sense organs purified claim that the ten [realms] are fixed, or that the ten parts of the true traces descend upon the ten realms in the same way, even up to the perfection of the fruit being equal to those hundred realms?

What would be accomplished by such accomplishment? What would the nature of the hundred realms correspond to? To what would they correspond as objects for the capacity of sentient beings? These are the hundred realms of that multitude.
If one has already been moved by another, how could it not be due to the purity of that mind? Thus, the Buddha-land is pure.

Therefore, from the very first moment of the mind, there is both cessation and illumination: because of illumination, the three thousand realms are eternally present; because of cessation, they are naturally empty.
In the initial contemplation of the mind, cessation and illumination are simultaneous; within emptiness and wondrous existence, the three thousand realms are fully present at every moment.
Throughout the day they are both absent, and throughout the day they are both manifest.
"Throughout the day" refers to the manifestation of this simultaneity.
Without moving from this single thought, one responds universally to all directions; as one bestows grace according to what is felt, the distinction between the pure and the defiled dissolves.

Since this thought encompasses the three thousand worlds, how could there be any movement? Responding universally to the various capacities of sentient beings, non-mindfulness is itself universal response.
When bestowing grace according to what is felt, how can purity or impurity be restricted?
Because both purity and defilement are transcended, one relies on emptiness and the Middle Way; yet, through emptiness and the Middle Way, one transforms defilement into purity.
Although transformation is said to occur within emptiness and the Middle Way, this wondrous provisional reality is such that not even a speck of dust can be altered.
They vanish of their own accord into space.
When defilement and purity are thus observed, one is said to have attained realization; as the illness departs, the medicine is discarded, and all is swept away.
The essence of the wondrous nature is naturally so.
This is established through the gate of the non-duality of cause and effect.
Without the aforementioned cause and effect, this function could not be accomplished; they follow one another and depend upon each other, never for a moment separated.

Sixth is the gate of the non-duality of the environment and its inhabitants: having already realized that the *śūnyatā* (emptiness) and the one substance are non-dual, it is truly because [this unity] has existed from the beginningless past.
Contemplate the three thousand worlds.

Vairocana is not limited by being all-pervasive, and the myriad sentient beings are not limited by being localized; yet within that pervasiveness and localization, their distinct natures are inherently pure and one.

When the fruit is realized, there is no realization to be attained; by taking that localized nature as the object, one uses the fruit to verify the cause, thereby manifesting the cause through the fruit.
Since the fundamental existence is all-pervasive and not dependent on causes, from what could there be further proof?
Within the three thousandfold world-system, two thousand worlds constitute the primary lands and one thousand belong to the supporting realm;

since the primary and the supporting both reside within a single mind, how could this single mind be divided into subject and object? Although subject and object do not exist, the distinction between the supporting and the primary remains perfectly distinct.

The perfect realization of Vairocana is the sublime fusion of the phenomenal and the noumenal; this state of sublime fusion arises entirely from the pervasive nature-inclusion (*xingju*) that does not transcend the three thousand realms.

These three thousand realms of the phenomenal and the noumenal are themselves the principle of the Three Truths. Where does this reality truly reside? It resides within every deluded moment of consciousness.
At each and every instant, the nature manifests such that the phenomenal and the noumenal are perfectly distinct, yet both subject and object are utterly transcended.

This is because, within the names and contemplative practices of the rational nature (*dharmatā*), there already exists the non-dual characteristic of the mutual interpenetration of the environment and its inhabitants;

thus, the causes and effects of self and others mutually encompass one another. Although sentient beings have not yet manifested the fruit within this principle, everything without exception is none other than the wondrous realm of Vairocana.

The three [levels] all possess consciousness, yet their principles are not the same. The stage of names (*nāma*), the stage of contemplative practice (*manasikāra*), and the stage of practice through understanding (*adhimukti*) differ;
although they exist, though they differ, none of them fully reveals [the reality]. However, the wondrous essence of Vairocana is dependently co-arisen and eternally fused.
Although everything is fused therein, it cannot be conflated; therefore, distinctions are made in accordance with this principle.
However, one must further understand that the essence of all Buddha-dharmas is not pervasive yet pervades all; the rational nature of sentient beings is not limited yet is limited;

it remains unchanged from beginning to end, and there is no obstruction between the Great and the Small. Since the principle of cause and effect is identical, what distinction is there between the primary and the secondary (the environment and the inhabitants)?

(As seen in the previous note), therefore, the pure and impure lands, the superior and inferior bodies, the dust-body and the Dharma-body are equal in measure, and the dusty realm and the quiescent [realm] are likewise.
Since light is without differentiation, then within each atom and each buddha-field there are all buddha-fields;
within each atom and each body there are all bodies—vast and subtle, superior and inferior, inconceivable, and pure or impure locations that are inexhaustible.
The wondrous realm of the Three Truths—emptiness, provisionality, and the Middle—is realized through contemplation that accords with nature and adapts to circumstances.

How could there be fixed locations or boundaries? Even the most subtle of bodies is not a substantial entity; how then could it give rise to [the perception of] lands? Though the lands may be minute, they are not merely physical territories;

how then could they exist without principle? This correspondence between the one and the many, where bodies and lands interpenetrate in infinite layers, accords with emptiness and provisionality, and is thus manifested through cultivation and realization.

The wondrous contemplation of the Middle, conjoined with the principle of the fruit of non-differentiation—the Great Teaching of the Lotus Sūtra, the gate of non-duality—is, when perfected, wondrously in accord with the nature (*dharmatā*).

If it were not for the three thousand realms of emptiness, provisionality, and the middle, how could such sovereign function be accomplished? Only in this way can one know that [the nature of] birth-and-death and Buddhahood are one.
The phenomena and principles of self and other mutually encompass one another.
If the three thousand realms did not encompass all objects, they would not be pervasive;

because the objects of the empty, the provisional, and the middle are not themselves the nature, it is necessary for the three thousand realms to be entirely within the empty, the provisional, and the middle to perceive the true reality (*dharmatā*) of all phenomena. Since the mind arises from the essence of the Buddha’s body, they are fundamentally equal and one.
When the ultimate transcendence and the wondrous fusion both lead to the Buddha-way, one attains the state where "one encompasses all" and "all encompass one.
It is for this reason that the *Lotus Sūtra*’s great undertaking exclusively reveals this principle; from antiquity until now, it has rarely been encountered, being unique unto itself.

The present school’s interpretation takes this wondrous intent as its core, using the Three Thousand Worlds (*sanqian*) as its guiding compass; it may truly be said to fully open up the provisional and manifest the real.

The title of the *Sūtra on the Principle of the Non-differentiation of the Three Ultimate Realms* describes the wondrous name of the *Myōhō-kyō* (Wonderful Dharma Sutra) as an inconceivable principle.
Briefly citing the realms and suchness, it fully encompasses the three thousand worlds. It praises the Dharma as wondrous because the Dharma itself is solely wondrous.

Thus, the commentary on the "Wondrous Realm" states that the three thousand worlds are themselves the nature of emptiness and the cause of awakening; the meaning of this passage is clear from the preceding text.
Furthermore, it is said that not a single thought-moment transcends the three thousand worlds as emptiness, provisionality, and the Middle; yet when this point is thus revealed,
at every stage scholars fail to perceive it, instead clinging to the existence or non-existence of the three thousand, attacking one another, violating the Patriarchs, betraying the School,
and becoming enemies of the Dharma— how can this be endured?
This is established through the gate of the non-duality of defilement and purity.
Since the pure functions of all the sages arise from the innate endowment, once the contemplation of the initial mind is attained, the stages are manifested in a single thought-moment;
only then do the defiled and the pure, the support and the supported, merge and mutually constitute one another.
Seventh, regarding the gate of the non-duality of self and others: the act of benefiting others according to their capacities relies upon the fundamental source;
that fundamental source refers to the single nature being fully endowed with both self and others, such that upon reaching the stage of fruition, the self itself benefits others.
The single nature of self and others has existed from the beginning; since this fundamental reality is my own mind, how could self and others be distinct?

As soon as there is a response to a stimulus, it is met without the slightest deviation. This is not something achieved through cultivation; it is truly the natural state of the one fundamental source.
Regarding the three virtues of the principle-nature, the three truths, and the three thousand [realms]:
the three virtues of the principle-nature demonstrate its essential substance; the three truths and three thousand realms manifest its perfect completeness.

Only when each and every element is perfectly complete as the substance of the three thousand realms can one attain the realization of the fruit and perform activities in accordance with the nature to benefit oneself and others. How could there be...?
Second, the distinction:
one's own practice is solely within the void, while benefiting others extends to the objects of the three thousandfold world.
Since the three truths are already a single mind, how could there be any difference between self and other? Do not pursue the literal words with biased views.
The responses do not deviate from the non-dual intent;

the infinite capacities of sentient beings do not transcend the three thousand realms. Though the modes of response are manifold, they do not exceed the ten realms. The transformations and manifestations do not emerge outside of a single thought-moment;
the lands and lands mutually arising do not transcend the land of serene light.

The three thousand realms encompass the capacities of all beings, and the ten realms unify the manifestations of response and transformation; though the terminology differs, the resonance between stimulus and response is entirely equal.
Manifestations and transformations do not depart from a single thought-moment, and the lands do not mutually transcend the *jigō* (寂光, quiescent light).

Is this not the state where the whole nature is identical to the principle-nature? When one uses this as a mirror to reflect upon the appearances of self and other, how could they possibly exist? Every gate merges with the title.
The essential point is this:

because sentient beings possess the three thousand realms as their inherent principle (*li*), they are able to elicit the response of the Buddhas; and because the Buddhas fulfill the three thousand realms through that same principle, they are able to respond.

This response is all-pervasive and the capacity for it is all-pervasive; thus, they joyfully attend to each being without error or deficiency. How could this be otherwise? It is like a mirror manifesting images: the mirror possesses the capacity to manifest images.
The principle of this physical form possesses the nature of having a manifested image.

The principle of life is identical to that of the Buddha, yet the response of the Buddha’s realization is equal to that of sentient beings; as soon as one rejoices, he arrives, like a shadow following a form.
Some might say this is not so, asking: "For what purpose was the analogy of the mirror-image set forth in the sūtras and śāstras? As for the mirror—
The principle of the manifestation of phenomena is like the Buddha’s principle of the three thousand realms; the nature of the arising of forms is like the arising of the three thousand realms.

When the principle is invoked and the response is felt, the interaction of the Way is harmonious and joyful, without the slightest discrepancy. The phenomenon and the principle correspond to one another, like a box and its lid fitting together.
How can one not believe this?
If a single form cannot manifest its image when facing a mirror, then the principle of the mirror would be exhausted and the phenomenon of form would remain unexplained;
yet if there were a separation from the mirror, such a principle might exist, for there is no form that faces a mirror and does not produce an image.
If a single capacity arises to respond to an inducement but does not go forth to meet it, then the essence of the response would be finite and its manifestation in phenomena would be obstructed.

If it were separated from a mirror, such a principle might exist; however, since every form that faces it is reflected without exception, we know by contrast that the response is nowhere non-pervasive and the Dharma is nowhere unpenetrating.
Nevertheless, what our school elucidates is that the correspondence between inducement and response is never at fault, for it arises from the living being.

The principle (li) and the substance (ti) are one and not different; this has been distinguished in the *Fuxing* (Sub-commentary on the *Sijiaoyi*), which states that while the *ālayavijñāna*’s perfuming and transformation according to other treatises is provisional, this [teaching] is real.

It is like a mirror that does not manifest images because they are obscured by dust: the removal of the dust depends on a person’s polishing, yet the manifestation of the images is not dependent on the act of polishing itself.
The reason a mirror does not manifest images is that it is obstructed by dust; likewise, the principle does not accord with reality because it is shrouded by delusions.

Although the polishing away of dust requires effort, the manifestation of images depends entirely upon what is internal. Similarly, while the contemplation of names and practices is constantly capable of eliciting a response, the delusions of view and thought must still persist.
For the manifest response to become clear, one must rely on the completion of effort; only then will the internal capacity be opened. However, this is the position discussed by our own school.
When the responses and interactions are combined, they form thirty-six propositions; what single dharma among them is not appropriate?
It is simply to manifest that the wondrous capacity for response lies in the perfection of its function.
Observe the Dharma through this analogy.
The character "guan" (觀) is pronounced in the level tone (*ping sheng*).

Its general purport can be understood as follows: one should know that although the principle (*li*) is inherently complete within both self and others, it must rely upon the conditions (*yuan*) and the understanding (*liao*) to function as the merit for benefiting others.

Without the merit of conditions and understanding, how could the nature (*xing*) be manifested? Since the nature’s virtues manifest through conditions and understanding to produce the merit of benefiting others, there is no greater merit than this.
Furthermore,
it is only when conditions (pratyaya) and causes (hetu) unite with the nature (svabhāva) that one can, in accordance with that nature, designate the myriad phenomena; thus,
if they do not arise from a self-nature, they should have no fixed location.

Although the nature is fully endowed, it has not yet accorded with the common state; only when the conditional and actual causes conform to and unite with the nature can one universally respond by establishing myriad manifestations.
This stage of partial realization truly accords with this profound principle.

This is established through the gate of the non-duality of the [Buddha’s] body and its environment; as for the gate of the non-duality of the three karmas, within the gate of transforming others, the activities are divided into the three secrets, which receive different names according to their conformity with the nature of things.

The three mysteries are of one limit; how could they be divided? Although the matters addressed according to capacities differ, when presented as distinct, they should be understood as identical to the Dharma-body.
As a single entity without distinction, the gate of non-duality is thereby truly established.

The Mind-Wheel discerns capacities while the two [other] wheels establish transformations, manifesting bodies and preaching the Dharma without the slightest error. In terms of the person, they are divided into the Real and the Responsive;
in terms of the Dharma, they are divided into the Provisional and the Real. Regarding the person, the Real and Responsive are distinct;

regarding the Dharma, the opening of the provisional and the establishment of the real are distinct. In the past, when the provisional was bestowed, the person and the Dharma were not yet unified; therefore, this is a separation.
The preceding explanation clarifies that from the beginning until now, these three [bodies] are in fact one, with the person and the dharma mutually fused; this is evident in the subsequent passage.
If the two bodies were distinct, why would it say they are "identical to the Dharma-body"? If the two teachings were contradictory, why would it say they all "attain the Buddha-way"?
If there were only the Dharma-body, there should be no manifestation in the world; if there were only the Buddha-way, who would bestow the Three Vehicles?
Although the provisional means bestowed upon the world belong to the realm of expedient devices, they are eternally fused with the wondrous essence of the rational nature.

Since this sutra discusses the nature, the provisional, and the real as the correct track, and since body and dharmas are of one essence and equality, how could the three karmas of body and speech not accord with non-duality?
Even his body is non-body; his teaching is certainly not a teaching of body or speech. Equalizing body, speech, and mind, his mental wheel and material form are as one;
transforming without premeditation, he is eternally in accord with the ultimate, acting in accordance with the capacities of beings.

The ultimate mystery of his transformative activity is such that he does not stir from this single thought, yet responds universally to all directions; how could his unconditioned (avyākṛta) manifestations for the sake of others ever come to an end?

Is it not the case that the hundred realms are one mind, and that within each realm there is nothing that is not the three karmas? Since even a single thought contains the three karmas, how could they be any different?

Since the three karmas of the hundred realms already abide within a single thought-moment, how could the wondrous truth exceed this? Were it not for the revealed and clarified ultimate teaching, how could this be proclaimed?

When the fruit is fully realized, the cause must correspond to that fruit; only by believing in cause and effect does one come to know that the three mysteries have their source in the hundred realms.
Because the three karmas are all empty, provisional, and middle, they are appropriately able to respond universally as the fruit.
It is not said that the hundred realms are simultaneously empty, provisional, and middle; thus, the aspect of attaining Buddhahood in accordance with the nature has not yet been seen.

Is this not what is meant by the statement that each manifested form and each spoken sound is fully endowed with the three karmas of the hundred realms, such that these manifestations further produce further manifestations?

That all manifested forms and sounds are born together with the nature of mindfulness throughout the hundred realms, reaching fruition and manifesting through this very responsiveness— this is precisely it.
How could its application ever be exhausted?

Therefore, within a single thought-moment of ordinary mind, there already exists the ocean of the three mysteries of the rational nature; even a speck of dust of retributive form shares the same fundamental principle.
Only when this is realized as Vairocana can it be called the non-differentiation of the three.

The ocean of the three secret marks and the wondrous nature of Vairocana both point to the fact that the mind and form of ordinary beings inherently possess [these qualities], which accords with the scriptural passage on the non-differentiation of the three.
Thus, one knows that this subtle principle of non-differentiation must accord with the nature of mindfulness; the wondrous realm where mind and form are non-dual can be contemplated.
Therefore, the original text states: "Within all dharmas, there is entirely the nature of bliss. (Record)

Coming to the point where it says, "To conclude, one must open the mind; because within all phenomena (dharmas) there is a wondrous principle, one can then discuss opening [the mind] to point out to sentient beings the inherently existing treasury of awakening—the non-differentiation between Buddhas, sentient beings, and the mind.

Since it speaks of "all phenomena," are these not the form and mind of the nine realms? Since it speaks of "having the nature of peace and bliss," is this not the wondrous realm of Vairocana? Now, based on this...
The *Miaojie* (Exquisite Explanation) directly reveals this principle, establishing the essence, attributes, and function of the initial mind’s perfect contemplation;

because this observation sees that the nature of Vairocana is no different from the fruit, the *Fuxing* (Supplementary Practice) states: "The mind creates all things—the three [natures] are without distinction.
Since the principles and texts are so clearly evident, how could one dare to produce further forced interpretations of this principle?
This is established through the gate of the non-duality of self and others.
Regarding the ninth gate, the non-duality of the provisional and the real: the great wisdom of equality constantly mirrors the dharma-realm;
it arises from the rational nature such that the nine provisional realms and the one real realm are non-dual, and the real is again the nine realms while the provisional is likewise so.
Because the Real (śūnyatā) cannot be dual, it is one; because the Expedient (upāya) cannot be singular, it is said to be nine. This directly demonstrates their characteristics:

if [the teachings] were perfectly interpenetrating, the hundred realms would be eternally so, and though they are nominally called "a hundred realms," their single nature would be without differentiation.

Yet, when the various dispositions of sentient beings are obstructed and hindered, the Expedient and the Real diverge. If one relies on this present sutra to reveal this ultimate principle, all are of one Buddha Vehicle.

The wondrous nature of emptiness, the provisional, and the middle is such that Devadatta attained the prediction of enlightenment by awakening to this, and the Dragon Girl became a Buddha by comprehending it;
both cases arose from great wisdom harmonizing with the Dharma-realm through the correct standard of the provisional and the real.
The provisional and the ultimate are mutually interfused; within a single thought-moment of the hundred realms, they are beyond discrimination, spontaneously and eternally so.
If discrimination arises, this essential principle is entirely lost; spontaneous suchness exists only in the state of transcending thought.
The ultimate fruit arises from accords with the fundamental principle of oneness; it is neither provisional nor real, yet it is both provisional and real. This is just as previously described:

through the mastery of the mind-wheel, one causes body and speech to respond to the capacities of beings according to what is provisional and real. Since the three karmas are unified in a single thought-moment without contradicting the provisional and the real, they are applied without movement;
how could there be any separation or distinction between them?
The principle of the "neither-nor" (ubhayānta-vinirmukta) does not differ from the provisional and the real; the response of the provisional and the real is entirely the "neither-nor.
When explained in opposition, they are designated as "provisional" and "real"; when manifested in person, they are named "True" and "Responsive.
The principle of the three karmas is identical [to this], such that the provisional and the real are in profound union. This constitutes the gate of the non-duality of the three karmas.
Regarding the tenth gate, "The Non-duality of Receiving Moistening": The nature of phenomena is fundamentally endowed with both the provisional and the real.
Since this inherent endowment of the provisional and the real is not distinct from the fundamental nature itself, their manifestation through perfuming arises entirely from that nature.
The beginningless perfuming is either real or provisional; whether provisional or real, it is fundamentally equal by virtue of perfuming.
