Although the nature is inherently present, it does not manifest without perfuming. As for what is perfumed, it is perfumed back into the single nature;

thus, the nature and the perfuming combine to give rise to manifestation. What was previously obscure is now clear: the Buddha-seed of all sentient beings arises from causes and conditions through the instruction of the Teacher.

Based on the entire nature of manifest form (*vijñapti-rūpa*), the names "cultivation" (*bhāvanā*) and "arousing" (*samutthāna*) are established; for if one does not receive the sublime teaching, there is no way to arouse this nature.
Even if it were to arise, it would merely constitute a provisional separation, leaving the six realms and the three vehicles in their delusion, from which they could not recover.

When meeting with the proper conditions, it forms habits; this is what is required for the fulfillment of vows and practices. If there were no fundamental cause, even perfuming would be in vain. That meeting with perfuming results in differences does not arise from a difference in nature.

If the formation of habits differs—as in the case of the three types of grasses and two types of trees—then their functional effects will differ. Likewise, the moisture provided by the teachings of the two provisional vehicles will also differ accordingly.
Now, although this sutra has been established as a single ground, all who receive its moisture share the same principle and return to a single consistency;

therefore, according to this sutra, there is not a single root of goodness that does not lead to the Buddha-way. Even bowing the head, raising a hand, or playing with sand as a child—all such acts are clearly reflected within this scripture.

Although their nature is without distinction, they must necessarily rely on illusion to manifest. The illusory capacity, the illusory resonance, the illusory response, and the illusory engagement—both the one who can respond and those being transformed—are neither provisional nor ultimate.

Since the capacity, resonance, response, and engagement are all like illusions, cultivation is entirely within the nature; the principle must be like an illusion, even though it is precisely that very [nature].

Because the benefits manifested through illusory response are clearly evident, the capacities of sentient beings and the Buddha’s response accord in harmony; thus, throughout the Dharma-realm of quiescent light, there is nothing that does not manifest the Dharma.

Nevertheless, because the innate endowment of beings is neither provisional nor real, yet constitutes the capacity for both the provisional and the real, the Buddha—likewise possessing a fruition that is neither provisional nor real—manifests as both the provisional and the real in response to them.

When the capacities of beings and the Buddha’s response accord, there is no partiality regarding body or land; all are equally the eternal quiescent light, wherein there is nothing that is not the Dharma-realm.
The principles and logic are clear, yet the interpretation does not accord with the intended meaning; it is merely a matter of words upon which one fixates, providing no means for true illumination.
It is like water that is extremely cold—only when one drinks it does one know its nature. This requires clear understanding; what is the use of clinging to mere words?

Therefore, one knows that the three thousand [realms] are co-present within the mind-ground; they are no different from the three thousand [realms] of the Buddha’s mind-ground. The substance of the four subtle elements is identical, and the provisional and the real are equal in their benefit.

By understanding this purport of the sutra, one realizes that the provisional nature of receiving benefit is the wondrous nature of the three thousand realms within one's own mind-ground, which is identical to the fruit of Buddhahood.
How could the realization of the wondrous nature differ from place to place? The four subtle elements are of one substance, all born from the same ground;
the three types of grass and two types of trees are moistened by the same rain. In truth, there is not even a speck of dust that deviates from this, so how could a single dharma not be real?
To cause all beings universally to realize the Buddha-way—how could this be in vain? Therefore, the Sutra further states: "There is none..."
That each individual alone attains extinction is entirely through the extinction of the Tathāgata;
how great indeed is the supreme teaching, which nourishes all things and brings them to fulfillment!
This is accomplished through the gate of the non-duality of the provisional and the real; therefore, through each of these ten gates, one universally enters into both form and mind, and so forth.
Because they are all equally moistened [by the Dharma], the ten marvels (*daśa-mithyā*) are unified in principle from beginning to end.

The original text provides an explanation of the character "marvelous" (*miao*) but does not establish ten aspects of it; the marvelous has no beginning or end, and the nature and essence of the three thousand realms (*tri-sahasra-lokadhātu*) are not yet perfected.
Only when they are both perfected and marvelous do cause and effect, self and others, all share a single root across the ten gates.
The mutual interpenetration of each and every aspect of the dharmas is not a matter of deliberate mental effort; it is the natural state of principle itself.

Just as objects inherently possess these three aspects, understanding arises based on this principle and is therefore called "wisdom" (jñāna). Wisdom guides conduct, and conduct accords with principle.

These three factors correspond to one another and are non-different, yet they are differentiated through provisional establishment. Thus, stages of depth and shallowness are posited to distinguish between them and avoid confusion regarding these three factors.
This merely serves to verify those three principles.

Since the five chapters on the causes and effects of one's own practice have already been established, the marvelous [nature] is uniform and without distinction; the entirety of transforming others is clearly evident from beginning to end within this.
Thus, the stage and position of the Mirror-like Wisdom (ādarśajñāna) are one and without error, and the gate of non-duality is manifest before our eyes.

The five chapters below concern the arising of function through the three dharmas. Since these three dharmas are already established as the three thousand realms within a single thought-moment—and because emptiness, provisionality, and the middle have been realized—there is functional application.

If one understands that the Dharma of all Buddhas of the ten directions and three periods of time is non-distant from its original and manifested aspects within this single thought-moment, these ten gates are restated so that the practice of contemplation may be recognized.
The Great Ritual provides a wondrous interpretation that opens up the Buddha’s knowledge and vision; were it not for this, how could the sublime purport of world-transcendence be proclaimed?

Although one may offer the highest praise, it does not depart from a single thought-moment (*ekacitta*). If one relies on the present sutra to understand this thought-moment, then the sublime purport of this entire work will become radiant within one's own mind.
That the essence of the Buddhas of the ten directions is entirely my own original nature—this is truly worthy of belief.
In the *Mohe Zhiguan*, the "three thousand realms in a single thought-moment" is established as the wondrous object;

it directly points to the fact that within a mere flicker of thought, the entire nature of the three thousand realms is present, thereby establishing the Buddha-vehicle. Thus, the principle of the inconceivable is clearly evident in its textual expression. Alas!

If even the worldly artisan Lünpien could not transmit the subtleties of his humble craft, how much less can such be transmitted? How much more so for the supreme Way that transcends the world—how could it be easily understood? Nevertheless, the superior...
What is spoken of here is merely the "trap" (the means to catch the fish). If one does not embody the Way, it is like being without the fish once the trap has been cast;
one will fall into false attachments and stagnation. Therefore, the Great Meaning states: "If one wishes to practice, one must invariably rely on oral instructions. The present case is likewise:

if one wishes to understand the subtle purport, it is difficult to penetrate without oral instructions. If one lacks this subtle understanding, how can one put it into practice? Thus it is reiterated.
The ten gates enable one to recognize the practice of contemplation; the words for this are found right here. Do not fail to believe!
Since the title is thus, one may understand the symbolic pattern by taking the specific as the general.
The commentary on the title is the general, while the commentary on the text is the specific; the general and specific are mutually interpenetrating, and their wondrous purport is of one suchness.
